The approval made these scope mapping entries invalid, and evaluation ignores them until you correct the mapping:

New and changed tools are not made available to agents until you approve them, read tools included: the gateway approves nothing it pulls. The connection of a server, its policies and its resource type declarations are approved here too, and its tools stay blocked until then.
Policies and resource types waiting for approval
The tools of this server are blocked until you approve them.
The server has no registered tools.
Approved the connection of . Its policies and tools still need approval.

This tool comes from a foreign server that does not say how dangerous the operation is. The adapter is read only: you can approve the tool only as Read (read). A tool that writes or deletes data will not pass through the adapter, so do not approve it.
Server hints (untrusted, no effect on the choice)
The connection changed while you confirmed your identity. Check it again and approve.
The server names its own system in its manifest. Approve only if this is the system you meant to add: the gateway sends the users' credentials for that system to this server.
How the gateway should trust this server
With a trusted CA a renewed certificate needs no approval. Pinning accepts only this exact certificate, and a new one has to be approved here again.
Approving the connection approves neither the policies nor the tools of the server: they wait below. It needs a fresh MFA.
None: the connection is not encrypted.

risk and action: to be assigned by an administrator
Risk goes down: to . The gateway does not approve risk lowering.
The switch changed before you confirmed your identity (someone lifted it and switched it on again), so nothing was lifted. Check the new reason and lift it again.
Identity confirmed. Lifting the switch you picked before the confirmation.

A switch cuts off a server or one tool for everyone: within 5 seconds at the latest on every gateway instance. Approving a definition does not lift it, and neither does a restart. Switching off needs no identity confirmation; lifting does.
Switch off a server or tool
Administrators see it on this list; it does not go to the audit logs. Characters left:

will stop being available to all users and agents, on every gateway instance within 5 seconds at the latest. Calls that have already started are not interrupted. Switching off needs no identity confirmation; lifting does.
will be available again to users who have entitlements to it. Lifting requires fresh identity confirmation (MFA).
Identity confirmed. Check the form and save again.

An override is one Cedar policy that only forbids. It is for an emergency: it applies to the gateway's decision on a call, to every server or to one server, and it is read by all instances within seconds. Adding one needs no second factor; removing one does.
The @id annotation has to equal the identifier above. For the gateway the policy decides the call action on a tool; for a server it must not mention tools or the call action.
Use lower case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter or digit (up to 55 characters).
The policy is longer than characters.
Added the override . It takes effect within seconds.
What it forbids becomes possible again as soon as every instance has read the change. Removing needs a fresh MFA.
The policies changed before you confirmed your identity, so nothing was approved. Check the differences and approve again.
The policies changed since they were opened. Showing the current differences; check them and approve again.
A running server presented these policies, not the manifest the gateway pulled, and the version () comes from the server. Read every policy and every declaration before you approve.
Source: manifest pulled by the gateway, version . Pulling approves nothing.
First registration: nothing was approved before, and the tools of this server stay blocked until you approve.
The text contained hidden characters. They were replaced with markers of the form [U+XXXX].
A very long text is cut in this view. The hash covers all of it, so approve only what you can review elsewhere.
Not approving breaks nothing that works today: the tools of the server stay blocked. Needs a fresh MFA.
Identity confirmed. Your changes are back in the form; check them and save again.
The current mapping is shown below; your edits were not kept.

A group grants the resource scopes listed next to it to everyone who is in it. A scope is <Namespace>::<Type>/<id>; the type has to be declared by a registered server and the part after the slash has to match its scope pattern. The whole document is saved at once.
No group is mapped to a scope.
Saving needs a fresh MFA. If it is needed, you go to the identity provider and come back with your edits.
Resource types declared by the registered servers
A group name starts with mcp- and uses letters, digits, dots, underscores and hyphens.
Enter at least one scope, for example Type::Name/id.
is not a scope id. Use <Namespace>::<Type>/<id>, ASCII only.

has no scope pattern, so it cannot be granted; the gateway will refuse .
does not match the scope pattern of ().

The servers the gateway routes to. Add a server by its address: the gateway checks the certificate and pulls the manifest, and the server has no tools until you approve its connection, policies and tools on the Approvals screen. Removing one takes its tools away and refuses its calls. No restart is needed for either.
The connection of this server was never approved.

Review it on the Approvals screen
Refresh probes the server again and pulls its manifest. It approves nothing and needs no MFA.
Any host with any HTTPS certificate. The gateway reads the certificate and the manifest from this address and takes the server identifier and the system from the manifest.
If you fill it in, the gateway refuses a server that claims another system.
The address cannot be changed. Remove the server and add it again to use another one; a new certificate under the same address is approved on the Approvals screen.
The server needs a credential of the user
Saving needs a fresh MFA, except for disabling a server. If it is needed, you go to the identity provider and come back to this form.
Enter an address that starts with https:// or http://, for example https://mcp-notes.corp.local:8443/mcp.
An http address needs the "Allow plain HTTP" option.
Enter a system identifier: lower-case letters and digits, starting with a letter, 2 to 31 characters (for example jira).
Choose at least one credential type.
The type in use has to be one of the accepted types.
A service account cannot be combined with a user credential type.
Added the server . It has no tools until you approve its connection, policies and tools on the Approvals screen.
Disabled the server . Its tools are out of service.

Its tools disappear from the catalog and tools/list, calls to it are refused, and the scope mapping entries of its resource types are removed. The system and the users' connections stay. Removing needs a fresh MFA.
Identity confirmed. Check the form, enter the client secret again and save.
The systems that users connect to and that the servers reach through the credential broker. The client secret of a system is stored in the broker's secret store and is never shown again.

A change of the base address, the authorization or token address, the client identifier or the revoke address deletes the connections of all users to this system when you save. They are asked to connect again; nothing is sent to the system. Changed now:
A generic REST system takes either the tokens of its users or one service account, not both, and no OAuth.
User name field of the answer

The broker calls this path on the base address with the token a user enters and reads the user name from the answer. Without it the token is stored without a check, and the connection shows no account.
Scheme of the secret handed to the gateway
Basic makes the connection form ask for a login next to the token.
Required now. The secret is stored in the broker and never shown again.
A secret is stored. Leave this empty to keep it.
Saving needs a fresh MFA. If it is needed, you go to the identity provider and come back to this form; the client secret is not kept on the way, so you enter it again.
Use 2 to 31 lower case letters and digits, starting with a letter. The identifiers gateway, offboarding, portal, broker, prometheus, platform, admin, registry, adapter, internal and ci are reserved.
Use 1 to 64 characters; control and invisible characters are not allowed.
Enter a path that starts with a single slash, without a host, a query or "..", for example /api/me.
Enter the field of the answer that holds the user name, or a JSON pointer such as /user/login.
Use an ISO 8601 duration of at most 10 minutes, for example PT30S.
Choose at least one credential type.
The default type has to be one of the supported types.
A service account cannot be combined with a user credential type.
A token exchange system needs the audience of the token.
Enter the client secret again: an address or the client identifier changed.
Saved the system . The connections of its users were deleted; they connect again.
The broker deletes the settings, the client secret and the connections of all users to this system. Nothing is sent to the system itself. Removing needs a fresh MFA.

Set the shortest expiry that works for you. The token acts with your permissions in ; the portal does not extend them.

One address covers all systems you have entitlements for. The client shows the model tools named system__tool, and the platform routes each call to the right system. Nothing is saved here: the choices below only change the address.
This filter leaves no tool that you can call. The client will see an empty list. Change the selection or go back to the address without a filter.
The list has about tools. Tool descriptions take up model context and make tool selection worse, so narrow the address to the systems you need, or to read-only tools.
The gateway returns tools per page; the client must fetch the next pages, otherwise it will only see the first one.
The address will appear once the selection fits within the limit.

One session reaches all selected systems. Text from one of them, for example a Confluence page with a planted instruction, can push the model to write to another. Entitlements do not change, and irreversible operations still require a code from the Authenticator, but the reach of such an attack grows. For read-only work, choose "Read-only".
A filter does not grant entitlements. It only narrows what the client sees, so it is not a substitute for access restrictions.
With nothing selected, the address covers all systems.
Pick a few tools or exclude a few. A long list will not fit in the address; use systems and exclusions instead.
